title: JD Vance Backs Scrapping H-1B Visa Programme, Calling It 'Completely Broken'
excerpt: The vice president defended the administration's blocked $100,000 H-1B fee while a second federal judge halted its enforcement, escalating a fight that weighs heavily on Indian professionals.
body:
• Vice President JD Vance said he would be "very supportive of just eliminating" the H-1B visa programme, calling it "completely broken" in an interview aboard Air Force Two.
  • Vance accused technology and accounting firms of using the programme to replace American workers with cheaper foreign labour, citing a foreign accountant hired for $45,000 to replace an American earning $60,000.
  • The remarks landed on the same day a second federal judge blocked the administration's $100,000 H-1B petition fee, ruling officials had skipped required rulemaking steps.
  • Indian professionals, who make up a large share of H-1B holders, face the deepest uncertainty as the courts, the White House and Congress pull the programme in different directions.

US Vice President JD Vance on Thursday said he would support eliminating the H-1B visa programme altogether, calling the system "completely broken" in an interview aboard Air Force Two with conservative commentator Jack Posobiec that was broadcast by Real America's Voice.

"My view is the H-1B programme is completely broken, and I'd be very supportive of just eliminating it," Vance said. "But while we have it, what we have to do is protect American workers."

Accusing firms of undercutting American wages

In a video posted on X by the vice president's office on October 1, Vance said the programme had been "totally taken advantage of" by technology companies, accounting firms and other businesses. He drew a sharp distinction between hiring genuinely exceptional foreign talent and using the visa system to cut labour costs.

"If you're going to bring in an accountant making $45,000 a year to replace an accountant who is an American making $60,000 a year, that's not you using the program to bring in a genius. That's you destroying American jobs and defrauding the American people."

— JD Vance, US Vice President

Speaking to reporters aboard Air Force Two, Vance said he knew people were "outraged" about the visas, but argued that his administration had "narrowed the programme" more than any previous White House, according to HuffPost's reporting of the exchange.

The $100,000 fee hits another court roadblock

Vance also defended the Trump administration's controversial $100,000 payment requirement for certain new H-1B petitions involving workers outside the United States. The White House introduced the measure in September 2025 and extended it for another year on September 21, 2026. The vice president said the payment was designed to discourage companies from using foreign workers as lower-cost replacements.

"If you're just trying to replace an American accountant with a cheaper foreign accountant, then you're not going to pay $100,000," he said.

But on Thursday, US District Judge Haywood Gilliam in Oakland, California, temporarily blocked the government from enforcing the fee, ruling that US immigration authorities and the State Department had not properly followed the required rule-making process before introducing it, according to Reuters. The ruling follows a separate decision by a federal judge in Boston, who had also temporarily stopped the fee in June.

The immediate effect: the $100,000 fee cannot currently be enforced while the legal challenge continues, easing the financial burden on US employers and the Indian professionals most affected by it.

An overhaul already underway

Vance's remarks come as the administration pursues broader structural changes to the H-1B system. A September 18 executive order directs the Departments of State, Labour and Homeland Security to consider whether a sponsoring firm has recently executed — or intends to execute — layoffs affecting comparable domestic employees during the application review process.

The order also mandates that the Labour Department scrutinise previously filed labour-condition applications to identify potential regulatory violations. Separately, the administration has established a weighted selection mechanism that gives greater weight to higher-paid positions in the visa allocation.

The H-1B programme allows US employers to hire foreign workers for specialised occupations that generally require highly specialised knowledge and a relevant degree. The visa is widely used in technology, engineering, healthcare and other specialised fields. Under existing rules, a worker can generally remain in the United States for an initial period of up to three years, with extensions potentially taking the total to six years. US law imposes an annual cap of 65,000 visas, with an additional 20,000 exemption for applicants with US advanced degrees.

What's next

Three tracks will now decide the programme's fate: the courts, where the fee faces at least two federal injunctions; the administration's own rulebook, where the weighted selection system and layoff reviews are still being implemented; and Congress, where Vance's elimination call raises the stakes for any legislative rewrite. Employers and workers planning around the system have rarely faced this much moving at once.
